highlights.content: ![Hugging Face's logo](/front/assets/huggingface_logo-noborder.svg) Get trending papers in your email inbox once a day! Get trending papers in your email inbox! # Daily Papers ## by[AK](/akhaliq) and the research community ![](/front/assets/papers-by.png) ### [Skill-R1: Agent Skill Evolution via Reinforcement Learning](/papers/2605.09359) Agentic large language models often rely on skills, reusable natural language procedures that guide planning, action, and tool use. In practice, skills are typically improved through prompt engineering or by aligning the task LLM itself, which is costly, model-specific, and often infeasible for closed-source models. Skill optimization is not a one-step problem but a recurrent process with two coupled levels of credit assignment: a useful skill must improve rollout quality under current conditioning, while a useful revision must turn observed outcomes into a better skill for the next round. We propose Skill-R1, a reinforcement learning framework for instance-level recurrent skill optimization from verifiable rewards. Rather than updating the task LLM, Skill-R1 trains a lightweight skill generator that conditions on the task context, prior rollouts, and their verified outcomes to produce skills that steer a frozen task LLM. This preserves black-box compatibility with both open- and closed-source models while making adaptation substantially cheaper than model-level updates. Skill-R1 proceeds over multiple generations: at each step, the current skill induces rollouts whose verified outcomes are fed back to produce the next revision. To optimize this recurrent process, we introduce a bi-level group-relative policy optimization objective combining intra-generation and inter-generation advantages. The intra-generation term compares rollouts under shared skill conditioning, while the inter-generation term rewards revisions that improve behavior across successive generations. Together, these provide a principled objective for directional skill evolution rather than one-shot self-refinement. Empirically, Skill-R1 achieves consistent gains over no-skill baselines and standard GRPO across benchmarks with verifiable rewards, with particularly strong improvements on complex, multi-step tasks. ### [EVISKILL: Grounding Skill Evolution in Replayable Evidence](/papers/2610.05030) Continual skill evolution enables LLM agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on determining not only what to change, but also why a change is justified and when it should become persistent guidance. However, existing experience-driven methods can lose the behavioral evidence and task contexts supporting edits. Moreover, a global validation outcome provides an incomplete judgment of its constituent changes: locally supported corrections may be discarded with a rejected revision, while evidence may require further experience to inform useful updates. To this end, we introduce EVISKILL, an evidence-driven framework that organizes execution observations into Replayable Evidence Cards and synthesizes edits with explicit links to their supporting contexts. Targeted replay verifies these edits through re-execution and provides feedback for correction. Across epochs, EVISKILL preserves evidence and provisionally retains supported edits for further refinement, while global validation governs their incorporation into the final skill. Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across six LLM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. ![JLU-Deep](https://cdn-avatars.huggingface.co/v1/production/uploads/6852e7443025dde58d881cdc/aLNYeVDBhZdvh2l74MZ-f.png) ### [SkillMAS: Skill Co-Evolution with LLM-based Multi-Agent System](/papers/2605.09341) Large language model (LLM) agent systems are increasingly expected to improve after deployment, but existing work often decouples two adaptation targets: skill evolution and multi-age...

highlights.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. GKE Inference Gateway can run the llm-d router as a managed service and extend routing across clusters and regions, while autoscaling tools such as KEDA, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Kueue can manage queue depth, saturation and quota on shared accelerators. highlights.content: DataCenterNews Asia Pacific - Specialist news for cloud & data center decision-makers [![DataCenterNews Asia Pacific logo](/brands/dcn-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Oracle expands NVIDIA AI cloud with Vera Rubin systems](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/29/cloud-data-center-server-racks-gpu-clusters-ai-nodes-story-322950.webp) [Hyperscale](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/hyperscale) [DC](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/data-centers) [AI](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/artificial-intelligence) # Oracle expands NVIDIA AI cloud with Vera Rubin systems Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Mara Sugue](https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTg1OSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c35d782a2ad379dbb3ebd1d7a0269b918cf68f7f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/maraheadshot.webp) MARA SUGUE News Editor](/author/mara-sugue) Oracle and NVIDIA have expanded their AI infrastructure partnership, broadening the availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Oracle plans to scale OCI Superclusters with NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems to the multi-gigawatt level, while making Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs generally available on its cloud platform. The companies said the setup is intended to support AI model training, inference and software agents that rely on both GPUs and CPUs. The move builds on an existing collaboration around NVIDIA-based systems on OCI, including GB200 and GB300 NVL72 deployments. Oracle said its supercluster design combines NVIDIA rack-scale systems with Oracle Acceleron networking, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet components and BlueField-4 data processing units. In the Vera Rubin NVL72 setup, each rack links 72 GPUs through NVIDIA NVLink. Oracle said its network architecture can scale across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. It also plans to introduce NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8, an eight-GPU system in an x86 server configuration with two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 processors, 4 TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps of RDMA networking. The planned HGX Rubin NVL8 option is aimed at customers that want next-generation Rubin GPUs in a smaller configuration while retaining compatibility with x86-based applications. Oracle said this would give organisations another route for training, fine-tuning and inference workloads. **OpenAI use case** OpenAI was cited as an early user of the infrastructure. In Abilene, it has trained and served GPT-6 Astra on an OCI Supercluster with more than 100,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, according to Oracle and NVIDIA. "As our frontier models advance, we need infrastructure that can keep pace," said Sreekanth Pothanis, Engineering Leader, Compute Infra at OpenAI. "NVIDIA Vera Rubin on OCI gives us the computing performance and scale to accelerate model training and serve increasingly demanding AI workloads." Alongside the GPU rollout, Oracle and NVIDIA said they are addressing the processor demands created by AI agents. These systems do more than generate text or responses and often need to call tools, execute code and retrieve information between model interactions. Oracle said those tasks can leave GPUs underused if CPUs become a bottleneck. Vera CPUs on OCI are designed to address that by supporting single-threaded work and memory-heavy operations linked to code execution and concurrent task handling. The companies also pointed to OCI Kubernetes Engine as a way for customers to scale CPU and GPU resources separately. Oracle said its Acceleron networking hardware can also isolate workloads running untrusted code generated by AI systems. highlights.content: [![UF Monogram logo](/media/templates/mercury-10/img/MercuryLogo-OrangeBlock.svg "school-logo") News](/) School Logo Link [University of Florida](https://www.ufl.edu) For Faculty * [Faculty Resources](/for-faculty/) * [Senior Communicators](/for-faculty/senior-communicators/) For Media * [Contact](/for-media/contact/) * [Subscribe to UF News Releases](/for-media/subscribe-to-uf-news-releases/) * [UF Facts for Media](/for-media/uf-facts/) * [UF Administration](https://www.ufl.edu/about/administration/) * [UF Directory](https://search.ufl.edu/) * [Hurricane Hub](https://experts.ufl.edu/hurricanes/) # Engineering researcher seeks to prevent AI agents from going rogue Harrem Monkhorst Share * Sumit Jha, Ph.D., has developed a system designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue. * His ATLAS system scans an LLM and senses when the model begins to drift from the task and redirects. * The system works inside AI models and does not impact speed or performance. As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of working on their own, keeping them focused on their designated tasks is a growing challenge.  University of Florida computer science professor [Sumit Jha, Ph.D.](https://cise.ufl.edu/people/faculty/name/sumit-jha/), is working to keep agents from “going rogue.” Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands.   The research comes as news reports have chronicled AI agents gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder.  Jha, a professor in UF’s Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or [CISE](https://cise.ufl.edu/), studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, non-invasive tweaks to keep systems on task. > “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.” —Sumit Jha, Ph.D., professor, UF Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper entitled “Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI,” detailing a system, dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory.  The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system.  Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it self-generates. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information.    “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong,” Jha explained. “Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.”   Existing strategies usually involve policing an AI agent’s answers after the fact. The ATLAS system doesn’t require retraining the model, and it therefore doesn’t expend extra computing resources or slow the model down.   According to Jha, so-called task drift is especially possible for tasks in which groups of AI agents coordinate with each other over long periods of time.  “Say, initially you told the agent you’re a doctor, you are supposed to treat patients,” Jha said. “By day No. 7, the fact that it's a doctor and it should treat patients is now just one of the millions of things it ...

highlights.content: [Accessibility Statement](https://www.cision.com/about/accessibility/) [Skip Navigation](#main) # NewCore Wins 2026 Cyber Top Innovator for Bringing Human Accountability to AI Agents [![NewCore, the security-first identity platform for the agentic enterprise, rebuilt from the ground up for the workforce that actually exists today: humans, machines, and AI agents.]( "NewCore, the security-first identity platform for the agentic enterprise, rebuilt from the ground up for the workforce that actually exists today: humans, machines, and AI agents.")](#) --- ## News provided by [**NewCore**](/news/newcore/) Oct 29, 2026, 14:00 ET ## Share this article Share this article --- **Enterprise Security Tech recognizes NewCore's unified identity platform for human and AI agent access, which gives every agent its own identity, a human owner, and governance enforced at runtime** TEL AVIV and SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- NewCore, the agentic identity company, today announced that it has been recognized in the Enterprise Security Tech Cyber Top Innovations Awards for its approach to securing and governing an increasingly agentic workforce. The award highlights NewCore Agent Guardian, which brings governance and accountability to AI agents. AI agents are entering the workforce at a growing pace. They operate with enterprise privileges, access sensitive applications and data, and take action across multiple systems, often without a person overseeing each step. Identity was already the primary attack vector before agents arrived. Now enterprises must answer harder questions: which agents are running, what each one can do, how their actions are controlled, and who is accountable when they act? Traditional identity platforms were never designed for this reality. Enterprise Security Tech cited NewCore for governing AI agents with the same accountability and security controls enterprises already apply to their people. NewCore treats every agent as a first-class identity, right alongside humans, governed through one identity core. "AI agents are multiplying faster than most enterprises can govern them, and every agent needs the same accountability we expect from people," said Zohar Alon, Co-founder and CEO of NewCore. "No security team can review everything an agent does, and none should have to. Human judgment belongs on the sensitive actions, with policy handling the rest. NewCore enforces policy-based guardrails, eliminates standing secrets, and scopes every permission to a specific task. For the most sensitive actions, it puts human review and approval literally in the palm of your hand. Thank you to Enterprise Security Tech for recognizing this approach." **Every Agent Seen, Known, and Controlled** Traditional identity systems were designed primarily around human users and applications operating with relatively predictable permissions. Autonomous and semi-autonomous AI agents introduce a different challenge. They can initiate actions, interact with multiple systems, and make decisions at machine speed, often without a person overseeing each step. NewCore governs what agents can do, not just whether they can connect to a system. Key capabilities include: * **An identity and an owner for every agent.** Each AI agent receives its own identity, a defined human owner, scoped permissions, and a managed lifecycle. highlights.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. GKE Inference Gateway can run the llm-d router as a managed service and extend routing across clusters and regions, while autoscaling tools such as KEDA, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Kueue can manage queue depth, saturation and quota on shared accelerators. highlights.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Systematic review maps AI robotics advances and persistent challenges ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Systematic review maps AI robotics advances and persistent challenges](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-22333-750x422.png) Systematic review maps AI robotics advances and persistent challenges A systematic literature review published in the International Journal of Intelligent Robotics and Applications examines how artificial intelligence and robotics have developed across industries, drawing on studies published between 2018 and 2026. The review, conducted by Muhammad Hasnain, Fazal Ur Rehman, Yu-Chen Hu, Chang-Ming Wu and Saira Shakoor, followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to identify, screen and select relevant research in a structured way. The search strategy produced a final set of 119 studies that met the authors’ inclusion and exclusion criteria. Rather than reporting new experimental results, the paper synthesises what this existing literature says about where AI-driven robotics is being deployed, what obstacles remain, and which research directions the field is expected to pursue next. According to the review, robotics and AI are widely used across manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, e-commerce, finance and entertainment. The reported purposes are consistent across sectors: automating tedious tasks, increasing production and improving efficiency. In production environments, collaborative robots are described as operating alongside human workers, while autonomous drones are used for tasks such as transportation, inspection and surveillance. Despite the improvements documented in the literature, the authors identify a set of persistent problems. These include data security and privacy, resilience against hostile attacks, the interpretability of AI models, and public acceptance of automation. Stakeholder participation, teamwork and interdisciplinary research are described as necessary to address these issues. Looking forward, the authors list several research directions highlighted in the literature: explainable AI, ethical AI, human-centered design, multi-agent systems, bioinspired robotics, and sustainable and resilient AI. The review concludes that future advances in these areas could improve the capabilities, safety and societal effects of intelligent systems. As a synthesis of 119 studies rather than a single experiment, the paper offers a mapped overview of the field’s state as reported in the literature from 2018 to 2026, along with the challenges and directions its authors consider most pressing for the next phase of AI-driven robotics research. **Subject of Research:** A systematic literature review of AI-driven robotics applications, challenges and future research directions **Article Title:** Recent breakthroughs in AI-driven robotics: advancements, challenges, and future directions: a systematic literature review **Article References:** Hasnain, M., Rehman, F. American multinational technology conglomerate Meta has initiated a US$97.5 billion financing plan to pursue artificial intelligence opportunities. The investment focuses on the infrastructure and compute capacity needed to support AI initiatives. The plan includes an equity offering, which has drawn interest from cornerstone investors [NVIDIA](/tag/nvidia) Corporation, Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. ([AMD](/tag/amd)), and Broadcom Inc. This sum includes approximately US$37.5 billion in underwritten public offerings. Advt These offerings comprise about US$25 billion in Class A common stock and around US$12.5 billion in depositary shares representing Preferred Stock. Meta also intends to launch an at-the-market (ATM) program worth about US$60 billion when trading on its Class C common stock begins, though "there can be no assurance" it will be established. NVIDIA, AMD, and Broadcom could collectively purchase up to US$5 billion of Class A common stock, according to Meta. NVIDIA will invest US$3 billion in Meta’s equity offering and expand its partnership with Meta for AI agents and Muse family models. Jensen Huang, NVIDIA founder and Chief Executive Officer, stated that AI agents represent a new computing paradigm. He noted that NVIDIA and Meta are expanding their partnership to optimise computing infrastructure for efficient and secure AI agents. Meta will expand its deployment of NVIDIA Vera Rubin and Vera CPU solutions. The company will also consider other collaborations related to monitoring, structured, unstructured, and graph data processing, NVIDIA said. Advt AMD technologies are also supporting Meta’s Muse platform, with the chipmaker stating its Helios and EPYC products are powering the agentic platform. AMD has committed US$1 billion to Meta’s equity offering. Mark Zuckerberg, Meta founder and Chief Executive Officer, highlighted Meta’s significant investments in computing power. He added that AMD plays an important role in enabling personal superintelligence for everyone. Advt Meta expects its [capital expenditure](/tag/capital+expenditure) to be between US$135 billion and US$145 billion in 2026. In its third quarter, Meta reported revenue of US$64.6 billion and a net income of US$9.9 billion. The company expects to nearly double its total infrastructure capacity year-on-year in that same period. Meta is building as many as four data center [superclusters](/tag/superclusters), each with over 1 GW of capacity. The campaign began on October 17, 2026, and involved ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI framework, alongside the Chinese-developed DeepSeek large language model (LLM) and a second commercial LLM. The operation targeted government institutions, pharmaceutical companies, semiconductor organisations, defence entities and telecommunications providers. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team observed exploitation activity from a single ARTEX controller directed against organisations in at least 14 countries over an 11-day period. The activity included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, as well as US-based organisations in several strategic industries. The cybersecurity company confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organisations, where the attackers gained access, deployed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and conducted further credential spraying, network scanning and reconnaissance. At least 12 additional organisations were subjected to password-spraying and credential-scanning activity, including US think tanks and European government entities. **Broad targeting** VAPOR PANDA conducted extensive intrusions against foreign ministries in two Latin American countries and likely compromised a third. The group also prepared target files for foreign ministries in Central America and Asia. In the Middle East, the adversary compromised an interior ministry. Another operation focused on a European country, targeting its foreign ministry, presidency and prime minister's office, alongside defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities. The campaign also involved 19 US-based organisations across the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defence, nuclear and financial sectors. Telecommunications providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines were also compromised. The targeting represents an expansion of VAPOR PANDA's previous activities. Since 2021, the group has primarily focused on government, think tank, energy and extractive organisations across Europe, North America, Oceania and the UK to establish long-term access. As artificial intelligence systems become increasingly capable of working on their own, keeping them focused on their designated tasks is a growing challenge.  University of Florida computer science professor [Sumit Jha, Ph.D.](https://cise.ufl.edu/people/faculty/name/sumit-jha/), is working to keep agents from “going rogue.” Jha and his team have developed a system that can detect when an AI model begins to drift from its assigned task and steer it back without retraining the model or adding significant computing demands.   The research comes as news reports have chronicled AI agents gaining more autonomy and occasionally behaving in ways their developers did not intend. Recent incidents have included AI agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July, claiming to have information about an unsolved murder.  Jha, a professor in UF’s Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering, or [CISE](https://cise.ufl.edu/), studies how to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. He is working to engineer simple, non-invasive tweaks to keep systems on task. > “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.” —Sumit Jha, Ph.D., professor, UF Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering Jha and his collaborators have authored a paper entitled “Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI,” detailing a system, dubbed ATLAS, which stands for Algebraic Task–role Locking with Adaptive Spectral Memory.  The acronym hints at the dense mathematics at the heart of the system.  Jha and his co-authors, Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha, devised a system that works inside the large language model, or LLM, as it self-generates. When the model begins to drift from its task, the ATLAS system steers the LLM back toward the assignment, as well as its original responsibility and the latest shared information.    “An AI agent can start going wrong before its response looks wrong,” Jha explained. “Inside the model, it may already be drifting from the task, confusing its role or relying on information that has been replaced. ATLAS is built to correct that drift before it reaches the next message, so other agents do not build on the mistake.”   Existing strategies usually involve policing an AI agent’s answers after the fact. They operate with enterprise privileges, access sensitive applications and data, and take action across multiple systems, often without a person overseeing each step. Identity was already the primary attack vector before agents arrived. Now enterprises must answer harder questions: which agents are running, what each one can do, how their actions are controlled, and who is accountable when they act? "No security team can review everything an agent does, and none should have to. Human judgment belongs on the sensitive actions, with policy handling the rest. AI Agents.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # Systematic review maps AI robotics advances and persistent challenges ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![Systematic review maps AI robotics advances and persistent challenges](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-22333-750x422.png) Systematic review maps AI robotics advances and persistent challenges A systematic literature review published in the International Journal of Intelligent Robotics and Applications examines how artificial intelligence and robotics have developed across industries, drawing on studies published between 2018 and 2026. The review, conducted by Muhammad Hasnain, Fazal Ur Rehman, Yu-Chen Hu, Chang-Ming Wu and Saira Shakoor, followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to identify, screen and select relevant research in a structured way. The search strategy produced a final set of 119 studies that met the authors’ inclusion and exclusion criteria. Rather than reporting new experimental results, the paper synthesises what this existing literature says about where AI-driven robotics is being deployed, what obstacles remain, and which research directions the field is expected to pursue next. According to the review, robotics and AI are widely used across manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, e-commerce, finance and entertainment. The reported purposes are consistent across sectors: automating tedious tasks, increasing production and improving efficiency. In production environments, collaborative robots are described as operating alongside human workers, while autonomous drones are used for tasks such as transportation, inspection and surveillance. Despite the improvements documented in the literature, the authors identify a set of persistent problems. These include data security and privacy, resilience against hostile attacks, the interpretability of AI models, and public acceptance of automation. Stakeholder participation, teamwork and interdisciplinary research are described as necessary to address these issues. Looking forward, the authors list several research directions highlighted in the literature: explainable AI, ethical AI, human-centered design, multi-agent systems, bioinspired robotics, and sustainable and resilient AI. The review concludes that future advances in these areas could improve the capabilities, safety and societal effects of intelligent systems. As a synthesis of 119 studies rather than a single experiment, the paper offers a mapped overview of the field’s state as reported in the literature from 2018 to 2026, along with the challenges and directions its authors consider most pressing for the next phase of AI-driven robotics research. **Subject of Research:** A systematic literature review of AI-driven robotics applications, challenges and future research directions **Article Title:** Recent breakthroughs in AI-driven robotics: advancements, challenges, and future directions: a systematic literature review **Article References:** Hasnain, M., Rehman, F. OpenAI updates AI behavior rules with focus on human intent — Channel NewsAsia [Fedir Kryshtovskyi](/en/%D0%A4%D0%B5%D0%B4%D1%96%D1%80%20%D0%9A%D1%80%D0%B8%D1%88%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B2%D1%81%D1%8C%D0%BA%D0%B8%D0%B9) 29 October 2026 21:03 ![OpenAI updates AI behavior rules with focus on human intent — Channel NewsAsia](https://cdn-cabinet.ua.news/uploads/images/openai_updated_ai_model_rules_human_inte_1793300625901.webp?8073772 "OpenAI updates AI behavior rules with focus on human intent — Channel NewsAsia") OpenAI has updated its public Model Spec document, which defines the desired principles of behavior for its artificial intelligence models. The new framework is built around five values: fidelity to human intent, minimizing harm, honesty and transparency, human autonomy, and care. ## Human intent as the foundation As [Channel NewsAsia reports](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/business/openai-says-human-intent-center-updated-ai-model-guidelines-6504786), OpenAI called fidelity to human intent the foundation of its new approach. The company believes that models should understand what users, developers, and OpenAI itself seek and value, rather than merely follow instructions literally. The update is part of the company’s work to align AI behavior with human values. According to OpenAI’s plan, models should apply these principles in unfamiliar situations while remaining under human control. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel [Telegram](https://telegram.me/uanewsstream). ## Transparency and user control The revised specification provides that models should reduce potential harm, communicate transparently about what they know and do not know, and help users make their own decisions and achieve their own goals. OpenAI said that current models do not yet fully comply with the updated principles. The company is studying new training methods that could help models learn these rules. The approach resembles Anthropic’s Constitutional AI, where model behavior is guided by a written set of principles. The update was released amid heightened attention to AI alignment after OpenAI reported that an autonomous AI agent hacked Hugging Face during testing. According to the company, the incident showed how advanced models can break rules or bypass safeguards while carrying out assigned tasks. Get trending papers in your email inbox! # Daily Papers ## by[AK](/akhaliq) and the research community ![](/front/assets/papers-by.png) ### [Skill-R1: Agent Skill Evolution via Reinforcement Learning](/papers/2605.09359) Agentic large language models often rely on skills, reusable natural language procedures that guide planning, action, and tool use. In practice, skills are typically improved through prompt engineering or by aligning the task LLM itself, which is costly, model-specific, and often infeasible for closed-source models. Skill optimization is not a one-step problem but a recurrent process with two coupled levels of credit assignment: a useful skill must improve rollout quality under current conditioning, while a useful revision must turn observed outcomes into a better skill for the next round. We propose Skill-R1, a reinforcement learning framework for instance-level recurrent skill optimization from verifiable rewards. Rather than updating the task LLM, Skill-R1 trains a lightweight skill generator that conditions on the task context, prior rollouts, and their verified outcomes to produce skills that steer a frozen task LLM. This preserves black-box compatibility with both open- and closed-source models while making adaptation substantially cheaper than model-level updates. Skill-R1 proceeds over multiple generations: at each step, the current skill induces rollouts whose verified outcomes are fed back to produce the next revision. To optimize this recurrent process, we introduce a bi-level group-relative policy optimization objective combining intra-generation and inter-generation advantages. The intra-generation term compares rollouts under shared skill conditioning, while the inter-generation term rewards revisions that improve behavior across successive generations. Together, these provide a principled objective for directional skill evolution rather than one-shot self-refinement. Empirically, Skill-R1 achieves consistent gains over no-skill baselines and standard GRPO across benchmarks with verifiable rewards, with particularly strong improvements on complex, multi-step tasks. ### [EVISKILL: Grounding Skill Evolution in Replayable Evidence](/papers/2610.05030) Continual skill evolution enables LLM agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. Its effectiveness depends on determining not only what to change, but also why a change is justified and when it should become persistent guidance. However, existing experience-driven methods can lose the behavioral evidence and task contexts supporting edits. Moreover, a global validation outcome provides an incomplete judgment of its constituent changes: locally supported corrections may be discarded with a rejected revision, while evidence may require further experience to inform useful updates. To this end, we introduce EVISKILL, an evidence-driven framework that organizes execution observations into Replayable Evidence Cards and synthesizes edits with explicit links to their supporting contexts. Targeted replay verifies these edits through re-execution and provides feedback for correction. Across epochs, EVISKILL preserves evidence and provisionally retains supported edits for further refinement, while global validation governs their incorporation into the final skill. Experiments on three interactive benchmarks across six LLM backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. ![JLU-Deep](https://cdn-avatars.huggingface.co/v1/production/uploads/6852e7443025dde58d881cdc/aLNYeVDBhZdvh2l74MZ-f.png) ### [SkillMAS: Skill Co-Evolution with LLM-based Multi-Agent System](/papers/2605.09341) Large language model (LLM) agent systems are increasingly expected to improve after deployment, but existing work often decouples two adaptation targets: skill evolution and multi-age...

LLMs.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. GKE Inference Gateway can run the llm-d router as a managed service and extend routing across clusters and regions, while autoscaling tools such as KEDA, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Kueue can manage queue depth, saturation and quota on shared accelerators. People also ask ![site logo](https://d12v9rtnomnebu.cloudfront.net/logo/printer_friendly/techtarget.jpg) # Ways to manage AI model updates without breaking production All businesses, especially those that use third-party AI models, need a structured approach to managing model changes without introducing unnecessary production risk. ![Abhishek Jadhav's headshot](https://d1b6lhn2ymmy1x.cloudfront.net/journalist-headshots/TechTarget%20contributors/abhishek_jadhav-600x600.jpg) ![](/static/img/social_icons/share-icon.svg?045615291026) ![](/static/img/social_icons/share_dropdown/share-link-box.svg?045615291026) ![](/static/img/social_icons/share_dropdown/email.svg?045615291026) ![](/static/img/social_icons/share_dropdown/linkedin.svg?045615291026) ![](/static/img/social_icons/share_dropdown/x.svg?045615291026) ![](/static/img/social_icons/share_dropdown/facebook.svg?045615291026) ![](/static/img/social_icons/share_dropdown/print.svg?045615291026) ![](/static/img/social_icons/article_page/bookmark-add.svg?045615291026) ![Two white arrows turn clockwise in a circle on top of a server board.](https://imgproxy.divecdn.com/knSkfMyt3DDToQo29Gpk8jQQN83fqMRA1EGgM3xeDRA/g:ce/rs:fill:1200:675:1/Z3M6Ly9kaXZlc2l0ZS1zdG9yYWdlL2RpdmVpbWFnZS91cGRhdGUtaWNvbi1pbi1mdXR1cmlzdGljLXNwYWNlLmpwZw==.webp) ![](/static/img/play.svg?045615291026) Enterprise AI applications often rely on models that external providers supply and maintain. Businesses might control their application code, but have almost no control over the lifecycle of the underlying models. Any changes to these models can affect how applications understand instructions, generate responses, interact with tools and handle requests. For example, a customer support application might [use a large language model (LLM)](https://www.techtarget.com/news/LLM-build-vs-buy-A-decision-framework-for-LLM-adoption/834153/) to classify incoming tickets. When the provider updates the underlying LLM, the newer model might offer better reasoning capabilities but assign tickets to different categories. Model changes also vary in scope. Upgrades introduce newer capabilities, and version changes involve moving between releases. Deprecations require businesses to migrate before older models are retired. Minor version changes often require less extensive validation, but substantial upgrades can involve changes to prompts, integrations and application workflows. Model updates are a recurring part of operating enterprise AI applications. The objective is to manage changes without disrupting the business workflows that depend on them. Maintaining model inventories, representative evaluation data sets, controlled [deployment procedures](https://www.techtarget.com/news/AI-deployments-gone-wrong-The-fallout-and-lessons-learned/834199/) and predefined recovery options helps businesses manage these transitions. Businesses should build these capabilities into their applications and ongoing IT ops from the beginning. ## 1. The placement of this content is part of a paid service.*** | # PointGuard AI Launches AI Gateway to Secure Enterprise AI at Scale Distributed by EIN Presswire *Unified model routing, MCP security, and cost governance help enterprises control AI access, protect data, and manage spending* **We built AI Gateway so enterprises can scale AI with security controls in place, maintain performance, and keep spending accountable.”** — Pravin Kothari, CEO of PointGuard AI SAN JOSE, CA, UNITED STATES, October 29, 2026 /[EINPresswire.com](https://www.einpresswire.com/)/ — [PointGuard AI](https://www.pointguardai.com) today announced its [AI Gateway](https://www.pointguardai.com/ai-gateway), combining high-throughput model routing with AI-native security and cost governance. Integrated with the MCP Security Gateway, the solution helps enterprises block unapproved shadow models, protect sensitive data, contain runaway costs, and scale AI workloads across applications and agents. As agents connect to more models, tools, and enterprise resources, organizations need consistent controls over what AI can access and how it operates. In its Market Overview for AI Gateways, Gartner states, “AI gateways are essential components for managing how AI agents access both AI models and Model Context Protocol servers.”¹ “Every new model, agent, and tool connection introduces decisions about access, data, and cost,” said Pravin Kothari, founder and CEO of PointGuard AI. “We built AI Gateway so enterprises can scale AI with security controls in place, maintain performance, and keep spending accountable.” PointGuard AI Gateway brings together: • Approved model routing with automatic failover • Prompt guardrails and sensitive data protection • Semantic caching, virtual keys, and budgets • Identity-aware MCP tool authorization and inspection Its Java virtual-thread runtime delivered 50 times LiteLLM’s throughput in benchmark testing with thousands of concurrent requests. Hardened software builds and build provenance strengthen supply chain security, while unified LLM and MCP controls govern north-south and east-west AI traffic. Correlated telemetry connects usage, cost, identity, and security events for operational oversight. About PointGuard AI PointGuard AI is a Silicon Valley company providing comprehensive AI and application security and governance. Its platform helps enterprises discover AI assets, assess risk, test applications and agents, protect sensitive data, and enforce runtime policies across models, endpoints, MCP connections, and enterprise tools. Founded by industry veterans who previously built ArcSight, CipherCloud, and RiskVision, PointGuard AI brings deep expertise in cloud security, data protection, and risk management. PointGuard AI helps organizations adopt AI with the visibility, governance, and control needed to manage emerging risks. The update includes enterprise search with Gemini, broader model support, new NVIDIA-based systems, networking and security changes, and software from Teradata, Solo.io and Mattermost. The additions are aimed at customers in defence, intelligence, critical infrastructure and other regulated sectors where public cloud use may be limited by data sovereignty or security rules. One of the main changes is the preview launch of enterprise search in Gemini on Google Distributed Cloud. The service gives users a conversational interface to query and summarise data held in air-gapped environments, including text, audio and video. Google said the search tool uses retrieval-augmented generation, with indexing and interactions kept within the sovereign perimeter. This is intended to reduce the need for custom development in environments where analysts often work across compartmentalised information sources. **Model options** Gemini 3.5 Flash is now generally available on Google Distributed Cloud air-gapped. Support has also been extended to open models including Gemma and Mistral, giving customers a choice of models for different workloads on the same platform. Google said it is among the first large cloud providers to make a frontier model such as Gemini available in air-gapped deployments. They are intended to provide local compute for serving Gemini, open models and related agent-based workloads at production scale. Google said the change is meant to improve data movement to graphics processors and reduce bottlenecks in inference pipelines. Hardware-offloaded IPsec encryption for node-to-node traffic is available at up to 100 Gbps. Google is also expanding security operations support through integration with Elastic Security. Open Source AI.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/30/prof-sashikumaar-ganesan-story-323008.webp) [Open source](https://itbrief.asia/tag/open-source) [LLMs](https://itbrief.asia/tag/large-language-models) [Agentic AI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/ai-agents) # Google launches llm-d 1.0 for distributed AI inference Fri, 30th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Google and its partners have released llm-d 1.0, an open-source software stack for distributed large language model inference on Kubernetes. More than 500 contributors from 25 organisations back the project under the Cloud Native Computing Foundation sandbox. The release formalises a system designed to help companies run AI model-serving workloads across clusters of model servers, rather than on single machines or behind standard load balancers. Co-founded by Google, Red Hat, IBM and other contributors, it links model-serving tools from the PyTorch ecosystem with Kubernetes infrastructure used in production environments. llm-d 1.0 targets a shift in AI inference traffic from simple one-prompt interactions to multi-step agent workloads and reinforcement learning rollouts. These workloads can arrive in bursts, reuse long prompt prefixes and compete with interactive requests, creating delays and duplicate memory use when traffic is spread inefficiently across servers. The stack includes routing that tracks where a session's cached context is already stored, a tiered key-value cache system, and flow control designed to separate latency-sensitive requests from background workloads. It can route requests across vLLM and SGLang deployments, as well as mixed fleets of cloud TPUs and GPUs, through a single endpoint. **What is included** Version 1.0 introduces a set of stable application programming interfaces and a request path tested across multiple clouds and accelerator types. It also adds higher-availability routing and upgrade tools intended to avoid dropping active sessions during software updates. One new orchestration feature is DisaggregatedSet, which manages separate pools for the prefill and decode functions used during model inference. This allows rolling updates to move matching versions together while letting each phase scale independently. The release also adds an asynchronous processor for queue-based workloads. The component can pull requests from services including Google Cloud Pub/Sub or Redis, then route them alongside real-time traffic while using strict priority lanes and quotas to limit interference with interactive use. Another feature is support for time-slicing on Google Cloud TPU and GPU infrastructure. Google says this lets operators use otherwise idle periods during reinforcement learning workloads to run asynchronous inference jobs, raising accelerator utilisation from about 40% to more than 70% in tested scenarios. **Cloud integration** Google is tying the software closely to its cloud infrastructure, particularly Google Kubernetes Engine. GKE Inference Gateway can run the llm-d router as a managed service and extend routing across clusters and regions, while autoscaling tools such as KEDA, Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and Kueue can manage queue depth, saturation and quota on shared accelerators. The campaign began on October 17, 2026, and involved ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI framework, alongside the Chinese-developed DeepSeek large language model (LLM) and a second commercial LLM. The operation targeted government institutions, pharmaceutical companies, semiconductor organisations, defence entities and telecommunications providers. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team observed exploitation activity from a single ARTEX controller directed against organisations in at least 14 countries over an 11-day period. The activity included foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia and the Middle East, as well as US-based organisations in several strategic industries. The cybersecurity company confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organisations, where the attackers gained access, deployed the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and conducted further credential spraying, network scanning and reconnaissance. At least 12 additional organisations were subjected to password-spraying and credential-scanning activity, including US think tanks and European government entities. **Broad targeting** VAPOR PANDA conducted extensive intrusions against foreign ministries in two Latin American countries and likely compromised a third. The group also prepared target files for foreign ministries in Central America and Asia. In the Middle East, the adversary compromised an interior ministry. Another operation focused on a European country, targeting its foreign ministry, presidency and prime minister's office, alongside defence, justice, finance and intelligence entities. The campaign also involved 19 US-based organisations across the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defence, nuclear and financial sectors. Telecommunications providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines were also compromised. The targeting represents an expansion of VAPOR PANDA's previous activities. As of October 29, 2026, six families dominate the conversation: OpenAI’s gpt-oss, Google’s Gemma 4, Mistral’s Large 4, Alibaba’s Qwen, DeepSeek’s V4.1 line, and Meta’s Llama and Muse releases. Their terms differ far more than their parameter counts. Here is the core point. Open weight models publish trained parameters for download, but that is not the same as open source in the way software teams use the term, and the license decides what you can actually ship. The [deepset explainer on open-weight models and sovereign AI](https://www.deepset.ai/blog/open-source-llm-open-weight-models) covers the definitional split well. Applied to the field today, the split is stark: only four of the twelve model entries in our table below carry a license we could confirm as Apache 2.0 from primary sources. Parameter counts and API prices already get plenty of coverage, including our [DeepSeek vs Qwen vs Mistral comparison](https://shattered.io/deepseek-vs-qwen-vs-mistral-open-weight-models-2026/). License terms, hardware floors and release status decide the rest, and they move weekly. Mistral Large 4’s weights are due by the end of October. Qwen4 is still in training. DeepSeek swapped its Flash model on October 17 without changing the API alias. A team that locked in a choice weeks ago may already be working from stale assumptions. ![shattered.io](https://shattered.io/static/favicon.svg)· Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. It rarely hands you the training data, the full training code, or the data-filtering recipe. That gap matters for audits, for reproducibility, and for any team that needs to answer where a model learned its behavior. You get a finished artifact, not a recipe. OpenAI’s help center states the practical shape of this clearly for gpt-oss. The weights are free to download, they are meant to run on infrastructure you control or through a hosting provider, and OpenAI does not serve them through its own API or inside ChatGPT. That last point trips up newcomers. An open weight model from a lab that also sells a hosted API is two products with two sets of terms, and the hosted one is not what you get when you download the files. Running the weights yourself buys four things that a hosted API cannot. First, data stays inside your boundary, which matters for regulated workloads. Second, you can pin a version and keep it for as long as you like, instead of waiting for a vendor to retire it. Third, you can fine-tune with your own tooling. Infra & Chips.content: DataCenterNews Asia Pacific - Specialist news for cloud & data center decision-makers [![DataCenterNews Asia Pacific logo](/brands/dcn-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![Oracle expands NVIDIA AI cloud with Vera Rubin systems](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/29/cloud-data-center-server-racks-gpu-clusters-ai-nodes-story-322950.webp) [Hyperscale](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/hyperscale) [DC](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/data-centers) [AI](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/artificial-intelligence) # Oracle expands NVIDIA AI cloud with Vera Rubin systems Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Mara Sugue](https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTg1OSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--c35d782a2ad379dbb3ebd1d7a0269b918cf68f7f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/maraheadshot.webp) MARA SUGUE News Editor](/author/mara-sugue) Oracle and NVIDIA have expanded their AI infrastructure partnership, broadening the availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Oracle plans to scale OCI Superclusters with NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems to the multi-gigawatt level, while making Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs generally available on its cloud platform. The companies said the setup is intended to support AI model training, inference and software agents that rely on both GPUs and CPUs. The move builds on an existing collaboration around NVIDIA-based systems on OCI, including GB200 and GB300 NVL72 deployments. Oracle said its supercluster design combines NVIDIA rack-scale systems with Oracle Acceleron networking, NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet components and BlueField-4 data processing units. In the Vera Rubin NVL72 setup, each rack links 72 GPUs through NVIDIA NVLink. Oracle said its network architecture can scale across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. It also plans to introduce NVIDIA HGX Rubin NVL8, an eight-GPU system in an x86 server configuration with two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 processors, 4 TB of DDR5 memory and 6.4 Tbps of RDMA networking. The planned HGX Rubin NVL8 option is aimed at customers that want next-generation Rubin GPUs in a smaller configuration while retaining compatibility with x86-based applications. Oracle said this would give organisations another route for training, fine-tuning and inference workloads. **OpenAI use case** OpenAI was cited as an early user of the infrastructure. In Abilene, it has trained and served GPT-6 Astra on an OCI Supercluster with more than 100,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, according to Oracle and NVIDIA. "As our frontier models advance, we need infrastructure that can keep pace," said Sreekanth Pothanis, Engineering Leader, Compute Infra at OpenAI. "NVIDIA Vera Rubin on OCI gives us the computing performance and scale to accelerate model training and serve increasingly demanding AI workloads." Alongside the GPU rollout, Oracle and NVIDIA said they are addressing the processor demands created by AI agents. These systems do more than generate text or responses and often need to call tools, execute code and retrieve information between model interactions. Oracle said those tasks can leave GPUs underused if CPUs become a bottleneck. Vera CPUs on OCI are designed to address that by supporting single-threaded work and memory-heavy operations linked to code execution and concurrent task handling. The companies also pointed to OCI Kubernetes Engine as a way for customers to scale CPU and GPU resources separately. Oracle said its Acceleron networking hardware can also isolate workloads running untrusted code generated by AI systems. Infra & Chips.content: [![datacenters logo](/_icons/logos/datacenters-logo-header.svg?mod=2)](/) * [AI & Compute Infrastructure](/news/ai-compute-infrastructure) * 1 minRead # PreussenElektra, NVIDIA assess German nuclear sites for AI data centers PreussenElektra and NVIDIA are assessing former nuclear power plant sites in Germany for redevelopment as AI data centers. The evaluation will examine power supply, grid connections, industrial infrastructure, and available land for large-scale AI operations. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 29, 2026 at 01:15 PM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * PreussenElektra and NVIDIA are assessing former German nuclear sites. * The study focuses on power, grid, and infrastructure for AI data centers. * No investment plans or specific sites have been announced yet. * PreussenElektra aims to reuse industrial sites for new economic impulses. [PreussenElektra](/tag/preussenelektra), a German energy company, and [NVIDIA](/tag/nvidia) are assessing former nuclear power plant sites in [Germany](/tag/germany) for redevelopment as [AI data centers](/tag/ai+data+centers). The assessment will examine whether these sites have the necessary power supply, grid connections, industrial infrastructure, and available land to support large-scale AI operations. PreussenElektra will provide information regarding the locations and their existing infrastructure, according to a press release. NVIDIA will evaluate the technical and operational requirements of [AI factories](/tag/ai+factories) and potential site configurations. Guido Knott, Chairman of the PreussenElektra Management Board, stated that their former power plant locations offer valuable industrial infrastructure and prospects for future-oriented uses. He added that the collaboration with NVIDIA aims to explore how these requirements can be leveraged for AI factories, combining site reuse with new economic impulses for the regions. Markus Hacker, Senior Regional Director at NVIDIA, noted that AI factories depend on reliable energy supply, suitable space, and high-performance infrastructure. He believes former industrial sites provide ideal conditions for this and could be crucial for the next generation of data centers. Hacker further stated that the joint effort with PreussenElektra will examine how their locations meet the technical and operational requirements for AI factories, contributing to Germany's AI infrastructure development. The companies have not announced any investment plans or selected specific sites for development. Their joint assessment focuses on the technical feasibility, existing infrastructure, economic viability, and regulatory requirements for converting former nuclear plant sites into AI data centers. PreussenElektra is responsible for decommissioning and dismantling eight [nuclear power plants](/tag/nuclear+power+plants) in Germany and is evaluating redevelopment options as dismantling progresses. ## Comments ![Comment](/_icons/images/et-default-user.svg) What are your thoughts?

Infra & Chips.title: The many types of AI chips on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure - Techzine Global
Infra & Chips.titleZh: The many types of AI chips on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure - Techzine Global
Infra & Chips.content: A wide variety of AI chips will be available on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). In addition to variants of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin architecture, Google TPUs will be available for the first time starting next year; the same applies to the large Cerebras chips. AMD, Intel, SambaNova, and OpenAI Jalapeño are expected to follow, though it is not yet known when. Oracle unveiled a long list of hardware announcements at AI World in Las Vegas. OCI is adding or expanding seven compute platforms, and its own Acceleron network is also getting an upgrade. However, anyone looking to get started with AI computing power today still has relatively few options. Only the Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 and standalone Vera CPUs are generally available immediately. The rest is planned, mostly for 2027. It’s possible that this date won’t be met, though the succession of new chip generations is fast enough that some urgency is needed to keep the hardware relevant and attractive. The most notable development is the arrival of Google TPUs, which until now have been exclusive to Google Cloud. OCI will thus become the first hyperscaler other than Google itself to offer these chips. This is the eighth generation, consisting of two chips: the TPU 8t for training (which, according to Google, delivers nearly three times as much compute per pod as the previous generation) and the TPU 8i for inference. Oracle provides all infrastructure outside of the chip itself, including power, cooling, and networking. The rollout will begin in 2027 and is expected to grow over several years into a gigawatt-scale deployment. ## Nvidia remains the foundation Meanwhile, Nvidia remains the foundation behind OCI’s large-scale AI infrastructure. The Vera Rubin NVL72 racks connect 72 GPUs via NVLink and run on Oracle Acceleron in combination with Spectrum-X Ethernet, Spectrum-6 switches, and BlueField-4 DPUs. Oracle plans to scale these Superclusters up to multiple gigawatts. The Vera CPU instances are intended for the work that agents perform between model calls, such as tool calls, code execution, and retrieval. This is an increasingly important component of agentic workloads as they become more long-running in nature. In addition, OKE scales the CPU and GPU pools independently of one another. A smaller HGX Rubin NVL8 server with eight GPUs is still in the works. Oracle cites OpenAI as an example customer. OpenAI trained GPT-6 Astra on a Supercluster with more than 100,000 Blackwell GPUs in Abilene, at OpenAI’s Stargate campus. ## AMD, Intel, and a host of inference specialists AMD is supplying the E7 instances based on sixth-generation EPYC Venice CPUs, with up to 256 cores per socket. In addition, Helios racks will be introduced, featuring 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs and up to 31 TB of HBM4. Intel and Oracle also announced a multi-year partnership, including OCI X14 on Diamond Rapids with AMX support for FP8. No dates have been specified for either. The range of options for inference beyond GPUs and CPUs is also expanding. Cerebras will bring its Wafer-Scale Engine to OCI in 2027, designed for latency-sensitive agents. SambaNova SN50 will follow as well. Notable are OpenAI’s Jalapeño accelerators, developed in collaboration with Broadcom. These appear to primarily provide capacity for OpenAI itself. Additionally, access is already available to Quantinuum’s quantum computer, which was previously brought to OCI. The heterogeneous setup makes Oracle’s offering more versatile. These choices revolve around more than just price: Nvidia is said to be leading the way in training but may not be the most attractive option for inference. ## Acceleron must hold it all together To ensure all these chips receive computations in a timely manner, Oracle is also expanding Acceleron. The High-Performance Fabric brings RDMA to front-end compute, and NVMe block storage gains more interconnect options with up to three times higher performance. The Oracle Collective Communications Library distributes traffic...

Infra & Chips.content: DataCenterNews Asia Pacific - Specialist news for cloud & data center decision-makers [![DataCenterNews Asia Pacific logo](/brands/dcn-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![ORCA launches PT-3 quantum computer for business use](https://datacenternews.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/28/richard-murray-and-seamus-dunne-story-322732.webp) [DC](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/data-centers) [Quantum Computing](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/quantum-computing) [NVIDIA](https://datacenternews.asia/tag/nvidia) # ORCA launches PT-3 quantum computer for business use Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Sean Mitchell](https://datacenternews.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyOSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--a929a91c2a04d9af95ed98b14ed4d405bc70c1a7/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/IMG_3092.webp) SEAN MITCHELL Publisher](/author/sean-mitchell) ORCA Computing has launched the PT-3 quantum computer, which it describes as the first quantum system built for commercial quantum advantage. The first PT-3 is operating at the Digital Realty Innovation Lab in London alongside NVIDIA-accelerated computing. Infra & Chips.content: DataCenterNews US - Specialist news for cloud & data center decision-makers [![DataCenterNews US logo](/brands/dcn-new-logo.svg) United States](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.com) ![Enteligent unveils PowerCore stack for AI data centres](https://datacenter.news/uploads/story/2026/10/30/modern-data-center-ai-server-racks-gpu-cooling-story-323019.webp) [DC](https://datacenter.news/tag/data-centers) [AI](https://datacenter.news/tag/artificial-intelligence) [AI Infrastructure](https://datacenter.news/tag/ai-infrastructure) # Enteligent unveils PowerCore stack for AI data centres Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today) [![Joseph Gabriel Lagonsin](https://datacenter.news/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNSwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--675a9c66bfe11204f24f3bdaad09013f83135297/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/Joseph%20Headshot.webp) JOSEPH GABRIEL LAGONSIN News Editor](/author/joseph-gabriel-lagonsin) Enteligent has introduced the PowerCore stack for AI data centres, designed to move power from an 800 VDC rack supply to GPU voltage rails. The three-stage DC/DC conversion architecture is intended to support higher rack compute density as operators prepare for rising power demands from AI workloads. The design spans the rack, server and GPU board. Enteligent says this coordinated approach is meant to reduce the space needed for power delivery and buffering while managing heat close to the processor. AI infrastructure is pushing data centre power systems towards much larger rack loads. Enteligent cited industry forecasts that machine-learning systems could require more than 500 kW per IT rack before the end of the decade, while suppliers are also developing 800 VDC infrastructure for megawatt-scale racks. That shift has increased attention on how electricity is delivered from facility power systems to chips. As rack power rises, the physical space taken up by low-voltage busbars, power shelves and transient buffering becomes a more significant design issue. **Three stages** Enteligent divides the conversion process into three modules. The first, RackCore, is a 100 kW rack power shelf that converts 800 VDC to a 50/48 VDC bus. This stage removes the need for supercapacitor and battery backup shelves, according to the company. The second module, MaxCore, sits at server level and converts 50/48 VDC to a regulated 7 VDC rail. It uses a multi-phase, multi-path architecture intended to improve efficiency and simplify system design. The third stage, ChipCore, sits near the GPU and converts the intermediate rail to 1.2/1.7 VDC. The module has 16 phases and supplies the final point-of-load or vertical power stage, the company says. The modules can be assessed as a full rack-to-chip chain or used individually with compatible downstream power designs, giving equipment makers some flexibility in how they adopt the architecture. **System approach** The stack is based on treating the power conversion path as a set of linked electrical domains rather than a series of isolated components. In practice, that means considering voltage, current, frequency, distance and electromagnetic emissions together across the full conversion chain. Enteligent argues this matters because, at AI-scale power levels, the most effective design is not always the one with the fewest conversion stages. Trade-offs must be judged across conversion loss, conductor current, transient response, heat generation, filtering, board space and system certification. The company says the architecture could enable up to 50% greater rack compute density. That figure is tied to reducing the hardware associated with buffering and power delivery, which can otherwise occupy valuable rack space in high-density systems.
